learning_objectives.description: Write sums concisely using summation notation.
Understand and apply the linearity properties of summation.

other_material.content_plain: In this class, we'll practice using notation for expressing sums using summation so that we will be able to use it in our upcoming probability lessons.
other_material.content_latex: In this class, we'll practice using notation for expressing sums using summation so that we will be able to use it in our upcoming probability lessons.

other_material.content_plain: Anatomy of a Summation: in the expression sum from i=1 to n of a_i, the sigma symbol means "add up", i is the index of summation (the variable that changes), 1 is the starting value (first i used), n is the ending value (last i used), and a_i is the summand (the expression being added).
other_material.content_latex: Anatomy of a Summation: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\] \begin{tabular}{ll}$\sum$ & Summation symbol (means ``add up'')\\ $i$ & Index of summation (variable that changes)\\ $1$ & Starting value (first $i$ used)\\ $n$ & Ending value (last $i$ used)\\ $a_i$ & Summand (expression being added)\end{tabular}

other_material.content_plain: Summation Properties: let c be any constant, and let m and n be whole numbers with m < n. (1) Linearity property #1: sum from i=m to n of (a_i + b_i) = sum from i=m to n of a_i + sum from i=m to n of b_i. (2) Linearity property #2: sum from i=m to n of c*a_i = c * sum from i=m to n of a_i. (3) sum from i=1 to n of c = cn.
other_material.content_latex: Let $c$ be any constant, and let $m$ and $n$ be whole numbers with $m<n$. \begin{itemize}\item $\sum_{i=m}^n(a_i+b_i) = \sum_{i=m}^n a_i + \sum_{i=m}^n b_i$ (linearity property \#1)\item $\sum_{i=m}^n ca_i = c\sum_{i=m}^n a_i$ (linearity property \#2)\item $\sum_{i=1}^n c = cn$\end{itemize}

plain_text.question: Expand and compute sum from i=0 to 2 of (2i+1)/(i+1).
plain_text.answer: Evaluate termwise: for i=0,1,2 we get 1, 3/2, 5/3. Thus sum from i=0 to 2 of (2i+1)/(i+1) = 1 + 3/2 + 5/3 = 25/6.

latex.question: $\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^2 \frac{2i+1}{i+1}$
latex.answer: Evaluate termwise: for $i=0,1,2$ we get $1,\;3/2,\;5/3$. Thus \[\sum_{i=0}^2 \frac{2i+1}{i+1}=1+\frac32+\frac53=\frac{25}{6}.\]

plain_text.question: Write - but don't compute - the sum 2+3+4+5+6 using summation notation.
plain_text.answer: sum from n=2 to 6 of n. Alternatively, sum from n=1 to 5 of (n+1).

plain_text.question: Write - but don't compute - the sum 1/2+1/4+1/6+1/8+1/10+1/12 using summation notation.
plain_text.answer: These are the reciprocals of the even integers 2,4,...,12, so one compact form is sum from k=1 to 6 of 1/(2k) (equivalently (1/2) sum from k=1 to 6 of 1/k).

latex.question: $\displaystyle\frac12+\frac14+\frac16+\frac18+\frac1{10}+\frac1{12}$
latex.answer: These are the reciprocals of the even integers $2,4,\dots,12$, so one compact form is \[\sum_{k=1}^{6}\frac{1}{2k} \quad\text{(equivalently }\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{6}\frac{1}{k}\text{).}\]

plain_text.question: Write - but don't compute - the sum -1/5+2/25-3/125+4/625 using summation notation.
plain_text.answer:
For k=1,...,4 the k-th term is (-1)^k * k/5^k, so -1/5+2/25-3/125+4/625 = sum from k=1 to 4 of (-1)^k * k/5^k.

Think about these in terms of the patterns you see between the terms. In (b): the terms are always positive; there is always a 1 in the numerator; the denominator is always a multiple of 2. In (c): the signs of the terms are alternating (- to +); the natural numbers 1 to 4 occur in the numerator; powers of 5 appear in the denominator.

latex.question: $\displaystyle-\frac15+\frac2{25}-\frac3{125}+\frac4{625}$
latex.answer: For $k=1,\dots,4$ the $k$-th term is $(-1)^k\frac{k}{5^k}$, so \[-\frac15+\frac{2}{25}-\frac{3}{125}+\frac{4}{625}=\sum_{k=1}^4 (-1)^k\frac{k}{5^k}.\] Think about these in terms of the patterns you see between the terms. In (b): \begin{itemize}\item The terms are always positive\item There is always a 1 in the numerator\item The denominator is always a multiple of 2.\end{itemize} In (c): \begin{itemize}\item The signs of the terms are alternating ($-$ to $+$)\item The natural numbers 1 to 4 occur in the numerator.\item Powers of 5 appear in the denominator.\end{itemize}

problems.name: Example: Decompose a summation using properties

plain_text.question: Use the properties of summations exhaustively to decompose the summation sum from j=1 to n of (a_j - 3b_j + 7c_j - 4).
plain_text.answer:
Apply linearity termwise:
sum (a_j - 3b_j + 7c_j - 4) = sum a_j + sum(-3b_j) + sum(7c_j) + sum(-4) (by linearity property 1)
= sum a_j - 3 sum b_j + 7 sum c_j - sum 4 (by linearity property 2)
and sum from j=1 to n of 4 = 4n (by linearity property 3).

So sum from j=1 to n of (a_j - 3b_j + 7c_j - 4) = sum a_j - 3 sum b_j + 7 sum c_j - 4n.

latex.question: Use the properties of summations exhaustively to decompose the following summation: $\sum_{j=1}^n (a_j-3b_j+7c_j-4)$
latex.answer: Apply linearity termwise: \begin{align*}\sum_{j=1}^n (a_j-3b_j+7c_j-4) &=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j + \sum_{j=1}^n -3b_j +\sum_{j=1}^n 7c_j + \sum_{j=1}^n - 4 \text{ (by linearity property 1)}\\&=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j -3\sum_{j=1}^n b_j +7\sum_{j=1}^n c_j - \sum_{j=1}^n 4 \text{ (by linearity property 2)}\\\text{ and } \sum_{j=1}^n 4 &=4n \text{ (by linearity property 3).}\end{align*} So, \[\sum_{j=1}^n (a_j-3b_j+7c_j-4) =\sum_{j=1}^n a_j -3\sum_{j=1}^n b_j +7\sum_{j=1}^n c_j -4n.\]

plain_text.question: Decompose sum from i=1 to n of (2a_i + 3b_i - 1).
plain_text.answer: Linearity gives sum (2a_i + 3b_i - 1) = 2 sum a_i + 3 sum b_i - sum 1 = 2 sum a_i + 3 sum b_i - n.

latex.question: $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (2a_i+3b_i-1)$
latex.answer: Linearity gives \[\sum_{i=1}^n (2a_i+3b_i-1)=2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i +3\sum_{i=1}^n b_i -\sum_{i=1}^n 1=2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i +3\sum_{i=1}^n b_i - n.\]

plain_text.question: Decompose sum from k=1 to n of (a_k*k/4 + 9b_k^2 - 2c_k*d_k). (Hint: be careful - this is a bit of a trap.)
plain_text.answer: Be careful: k is not a constant with respect to the summation index, so it cannot be pulled outside. Note: sums do NOT distribute across multiplication or division. Anything depending on the index cannot be factored out! Applying linearity termwise yields sum (k*a_k/4 + 9b_k^2 - 2c_k*d_k) = (1/4) sum (k*a_k) + 9 sum b_k^2 - 2 sum (c_k*d_k). Note the factor k stays inside the first sum.

latex.question: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n \left(\frac{a_k\cdot k}4+9b_k^2-2c_k\cdot d_k\right)$\quad(\emph{Hint:} be careful - this is a bit of a trap.)
latex.answer: Be careful: $k$ is not a constant with respect to the summation index, so it cannot be pulled outside. \textbf{Note:} Sums do NOT distribute across multiplication or division. Anything depending on the index cannot be factored out! Applying linearity termwise yields \[\sum_{k=1}^n \left(\frac{k a_k}{4}+9b_k^2-2c_k d_k\right)=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=1}^n k a_k \;+\;9\sum_{k=1}^n b_k^2 \;-\;2\sum_{k=1}^n c_k d_k.\] Note the factor $k$ stays inside the first sum.
